title: Material Storage
summary: Stack, block, and store materials so they cannot slide, fall, or collapse. Keep aisles clear, stay within floor load limits, and keep materials back from openings and edges.
talking_points: Materials stored in tiers must be stacked, racked, blocked, interlocked, or otherwise secured to prevent sliding, falling, or collapse.

Do not exceed the maximum safe load limits of floors. Post the limits in pounds per square foot in storage areas, except on a floor or slab on grade. Posting is not required in single-family residential and wood-framed multi-family residential structures.
Keep aisles and passageways clear so people and material handling equipment can move safely. Keep them in good repair.
Inside buildings under construction, do not store material within 6 feet of any hoistway or floor opening, or within 10 feet of an exterior wall that does not extend above the top of the material.
Separate noncompatible materials. Do not store more on scaffolds or runways than is needed for immediate operations.

Bagged materials: step back the layers and cross-key the bags at least every 10 bags high. Brick stacks must not be more than 7 feet high. Taper a loose brick stack back 2 inches per foot above 4 feet. Taper masonry blocks stacked over 6 feet back one-half block per tier.

Lumber: pull nails from used lumber, stack on level, solid sills, and keep piles stable and self-supporting. Piles must not exceed 20 feet, or 16 feet if handled manually. Block or rack steel, poles, pipe, and bar stock so they cannot spread or tilt.
Keep storage areas free of material that creates trip, fire, explosion, or pest hazards.
site_hazards_to_check: Materials stored near floor openings, hoistways, or unprotected exterior walls
Floors loaded beyond safe limits, or with no posted limits
Used lumber with nails still in it, or lumber on uneven sills
Excess materials on scaffolds or runways, or noncompatible materials stored together
discussion_questions: How high can we stack lumber, brick, and block on this job?
Where are the floor load limits posted, and what is stored near openings?
What will you do if you see a stack that is leaning or unstable?

attribution.notice: Adapted from OSHA standard 29 CFR 1926.250, General requirements for storage. Reproduced with attribution for jobsite safety training; not an endorsement by OSHA.

flags: Every point verified against 29 CFR 1926.250: tier stacking, floor load posting and residential exception, aisles, 6 ft / 10 ft setbacks, noncompatible segregation, bagged materials every 10 bags, brick 7 ft and 2 in per ft above 4 ft, block 6 ft, lumber 20/16 ft and nail removal, housekeeping.
Citation 1926.250 correct and 1926. Attribution: osha.gov, public domain. No UK wording.
